1: The short version is I've spent my career developing systems in schools, learning change management, and now applying tech.

I started as a teacher in DC, then went to Excel Academy up in Boston. We were doing a turnaround. I was on the leadership team running culture and operations, and we took the school from 270th in the state to number one and got National Charter School of the Year.

We got hundreds of visitors a year trying to apply our model. There was a big demand for guidance on how to do it well, and it felt important, so I launched a consulting practice. I had the privilege of walking into over 100 schools over the course of fourteen years, finding and fixing problems, improving systems, and helping each school set priorities and execute them. I met them where they were and took them from chaotic to stable, stable to functional, functional to rigorous. KIPP, Achievement First, Uncommon, most of the Northeast charters.

Then I found a client I was really keen on, Collegiate Academies down in New Orleans. They had an all-means-all ambition, super high expectations and super high support for all students. After initial success at a single site, they couldn't replicate it, and I was brought down to fix that. We did it first as a consultant, then as chief culture officer for five years. We slashed suspensions while greatly increasing teacher retention and student and family satisfaction.
Then we came back to Brooklyn, because my wife is from New York and the plan was always to raise our two girls here. Or at least that was her plan.

While I was at Collegiate I kept a small consulting portfolio, and one of those clients became Brooklyn Lab. They tapped me to consult intensively, and it converted again. I was superintendent for just over a year, as a steward. We stabilized the in-person schools, built the remote school through COVID, and took both charters through renewal. Both were reauthorized, and we passed off as planned.

Then two years at the KIPP Foundation, bringing 28 wonderful but very independent regions into some degree of alignment on a national high school strategy, and handing it back to the regional teams, who run it now.

And now I'm doing a really cool thing, or at least I think it's very cool. I build custom AI tools for school leaders. They point me at a problem, and I build the thing that saves them the time so they can focus on the real work.

The happiest I've ever been is in a mid-sized, growing charter network with outsized ambition. That's what my research says you all are, and this role is a perfect blend of the tools work and that kind of network. So that's what brought me here.
2: Mandate authority isn't what drives change, not at any organization that attracts this kind of talent. The idea has to earn its place on merit, not on positional authority. It's not something you can build a dynasty on.

That was the situation at KIPP. The Foundation is the national strategy, support and oversight arm, but it has no mandate authority, and we had twenty-eight independent regions and forty-eight high schools. Nobody had to say yes, so we had to get them to want to say yes. It came down to three things.

First, we aligned on the problem and the goal. Every region was part of our listening tours and working groups. We showed people the problem, asked for their hypotheses, and workshopped them until we had a student-centered logic nobody could argue with: accurate, timely grades, non-negotiable, and a 3.0 GPA as the target, which was research-based, not our idea. Then we got clear on the one number we were going after.

Second, we piloted it, and we made the pilot a success. We shrank the scope, worked it with our influential champions, and publicized the wins, so it was attraction, not promotion. People wanted to catch up instead of being dragged along. "Why are they making us do it" became "why aren't they helping us do it."

Third, we involved ourselves in the implementation. We supported it heavily, including the school-based routines, like tracking our single number every week. Our regional support person was overseeing that at each school, and we checked in with them regularly, because every rollout was its own animal.

And we gave them what felt like a cheat code. We made their lives easier and got them quick early wins with push-button data reports. They may not sound like much, but they really were. We went from super obscure data to super actionable data, and with our weekly structures, those reports made leaders look good, because they gave teachers a feel-good, and that gave us early wins we could stack. It's leaning into an advantage, so the work feels new and puts some wind in the sails.

In the third quarter, 46% of ninth graders across all 48 high schools finished at a 3.0 or better, up six points. Best quarter KIPP had ever had on that number. All 28 regions and all 48 high schools adopted the strategy. There was an alternate path, and no school chose it.
We piloted the tool and handed it off. Now the regions are running the play. That's the exact type of work I love doing.
3: We took Excel from 270th in the state to number one and got National Charter School of the Year, and I think about it in three phases.

Phase one was stability. I came in with a mandate for change: an entire new staff, a hundred students, and a school that had stopped growing because things were in such rough shape. I was dean of students, forty percent of the staff reported to me, operations included, and I brought the consistency and clarity from my classroom to the whole school. I spent six days writing the playbook, my culture manual and my operations manual. My boss thought that was a crazy use of time. It became one of the most important things we did.

Phase two was the adults. We focused on the five dysfunctions of a team and built a really strong best-idea-wins culture, with rigor and engagement as the primary drivers, so we stayed academically focused.

Phase three was student ownership, student leadership, and a deeply held sense of belonging. The grades were theirs, the classes were theirs, the culture was theirs. Honor council, student committees, orientation leaders. On the first day of school we had kids telling new kids how overwhelmed they'd been, and that they'd even told their parents they didn't like the school. Where we ended up was a culture where it was cool to be smart. Kids advised each other. When we asked a question, most every hand went up. Kids were genuinely supporting each other.

We were building dynasties, not just teams. Twenty years after that initial mandate for change, Excel is six schools across two states, one of the strongest networks out there, and one of the most successful at scaling without losing its soul or its results. Its high school is in the top 3% of all public high schools nationally, and a student I had in sixth grade now has my job.
4: The best example is Carver, and the principal I was brought in to assess is now the CEO.
Ben Marcovitz brought me to Carver for a two or three day trial, and it was clearly a big question on his mind whether this effort to support Jerel was going to last.

I presented to the leadership team, and I didn't pull my punches. I named the quiet part, because it was the real problem and it had to get fixed. Jerel is one of the best I have ever seen at working with students, and we just weren't playing to his strengths. And the two of you are in a bad breakup. Nothing works until Mom and Dad get right.

We were willing to buck the inertia of how we do things, but not in a way that was disruptive to students. It was behind-the-scenes change: the roles, the responsibilities, and the relationship between the two co-leaders.

We got clear on the problem and the solution. Then we invested in training people and put Jerel on stage, so everyone could see it could work, and we stacked wins. We fixed the smallest action first. I coined a phrase, connect and correct. Don't let your first interaction with a human being be a correction.
We shifted the staff from adversarial to partnership, and part of that was sweating some things a lot less, and the more important things a whole lot more.
Two hundred students when I walked in. Eight or nine hundred now, in a brand-new building. And Jerel is the CEO.
5: The hardest decision was moving a leader I'd asked to step in, and it was hard because of what it meant for me: could I actually do the job?

At Brooklyn Lab, the original high school principal left about eight weeks after I joined, in a somewhat dramatic Friday afternoon fashion. A colleague stepped in at my request, and we both knew she wasn't an obvious choice for the role.

The high school was struggling, and I was the superintendent, so it was my call. Moving her meant I would run the high school myself, as interim principal, on top of being superintendent, in the middle of COVID and with the reauthorizations coming. We were untangling knots and doing forensic analysis on the data.

I made the call, and I ran the high school for half a year while still serving as superintendent. We took both charters through renewal at the same time, in front of the Board of Regents, and both were reauthorized.
6: The one I think about most is a time I had a fixed mindset, which is ironic for someone who talks so much about growth mindset and assuming the best.

At Excel I had an associate dean of students who was a wonderful human being and a true friend of mine. Out of the pressure, the need to be on, to move quickly, to survive and thrive, I fixed my mindset about him and never reanalyzed it. I found evidence to support my hypothesis and ignored the evidence that I was wrong. There's a time for that. But in years three and four I wasn't developing him to become a dean of students.

Then I learned I had to leave, and all of a sudden I had six months before he was the dean of students. I realized I'd failed him as a manager and as a friend, and that I would fail the school and the kids if I didn't figure it out quickly. So it became priority number one.

Clarity: I named exactly what he was good at, and what he hadn't been given the chance to do. Investment: I asked him whether he truly wanted the job, and I let him know I heard him. Training was most of the work. It was I do, we do, you do, with tons of support and feedback along the way and a gradual release. And accountability: within a month he was clearly meeting well-established targets.
He's co-dean there now, with one of my former students, and he's still one of the best I've seen do this job. I wish I hadn't been so eager to support my initial hypothesis.
7: To be any good at consulting, you have to remember exactly what it's like to do the work, stay current, and stay credible, and the way I do that is by doing stints in-house, not as a visitor.

I've built my career that way. In New York I was with Achievement First as a consultant for my entire consulting career there. Then I was at Collegiate for two years as a consultant and five years in-house, and Brooklyn Lab was intentionally a bridge to get me back up to New York, which is what they needed.

Consulting is where you help people do the work. It isn't where the work happens. The work is energizing, and so is being genuinely part of the team. I've done a good job of injecting myself, building credibility and building strong relationships, but there's no substitute for the full experience.

I've also messed this up. At Collegiate and at Brooklyn Lab I started as a consultant and then moved in, and both times I kept a bit of distance from the organization. It wasn't intentional, and I do it very differently now.

As a consultant I always did two-day visits. Day one was diagnosis, day two was beginning implementation, and I was constantly torn between setting the leader up to roll this out in front of their staff at 7:30 tomorrow morning, and cutting and pasting charts into a document. Those are the same twenty-four hours.
So it's about staying current, staying credible, staying good at what I do, and the network. KIPP was cool, but I don't need to tour the Fairfields and the mid-level Marriotts across the country.
At some point a decision needed to be made. A school can't break a promise to kids. A school leader can't break a promise to teachers. I can't break a promise to principals.
8: Right now I build custom AI tools for school leaders, and I think this is a special moment, one that can finally help us deliver on our promise, or make the disparities even wider. I'd like to be on the right side of it, not for reputation but for results.

There's a need, and I'm well suited for it. I have a special skill set in knowing exactly how schools work, how the variety of schools work, what the common problems are, and where leaders commonly struggle. I've seen 48 high schools at KIPP and a hundred or so schools as a consultant, and I've gone deep in a lot of them to test hypotheses.

I've always been a systems guy, and this is the next level. It's the leap from Excel spreadsheets to Google Sheets to software to dashboards, and AI is the next one, orders of magnitude more powerful. I've always been building tools like DeansList, and at KIPP I was already building them into the solutions.

And it's not just that people point me at a problem. I'm constantly in touch with my network. I can text a hundred charter leaders and ask what their problems are. What I kept hearing was time. But when I dug deeper, I heard two fears: the fear of missing out, and the fear of messing up, doing nothing or doing the wrong thing. My job is to help them.

So I asked, what's the safe, leader-facing, human-in-the-loop, efficiency play that takes the mundane off the leader's plate so they can focus on the transformational? I built tools to answer that, and as new clients and new problems come up, I build new ones.

These are just a few of the ones I've been working on recently: a coverage schedule maker, a chief of staff, and tools for attendance, enrollment and retention, walkthrough coaching and PD. The coverage schedule maker is built on two schools' real master schedules, and it's installed at one. My estimate is two to three hours a week back to the person running the building.

And yes to AI in any role I'd take, in the service of the role, not for its own sake. I'd bring the efficiencies to my own work, and my natural tendency is to share them. I lead a monthly working group of education and tech leaders on exactly that.

The long-term vision is to get leaders really good at this, and for me to stay back and support them. There will always be a need for an expert who can build high-quality tools quickly. If a principal is going to decide how to approach AI for their teachers and classrooms, they need to understand it first. Some need a place to start, all of them need time, and I can help with both.

10: Yes and no. I'm not the person who's going to know the twelfth grade AP government standards cold, but I've spent my career on the part that decides whether instruction works.

Culture is a means to an end. It isn't an end in itself. It used to be what happens outside the classroom, the systems and the struggles. Then it became how that supports what's happening in the classroom, and now it blends and becomes one with the classroom. I was in the room when Achievement First built the Arc of the Year in the mid-2010s, and then I carried it to Collegiate and into the schools I consulted with.

I've coached on rigor, too. As I taught leaders how to coach, I taught them how to teach: real-time coaching, observation and feedback. And you don't get anywhere in any good organization without a clear end point and real facility with academic results.

What I've seen most academic leaders get wrong isn't the curriculum or what great teaching looks like. It's four things. Do they have the personal systems to stay effective and above the fray, is their side of the street clean. Do they understand systems, adult leadership and change management. Can they analyze a problem, fix it, and lead an initiative for change. And do they know what to do with the teacher who has real issues with credibility and culture. Those are the four I spike in.
Where people often fail is in the non-academic parts of the job. There are a hundred instructional experts for every five legitimate, proper leaders who can lead people through an initiative.

I came up at Excel, and at Collegiate, which had the largest CREDO effect size of any high school in the country. At KIPP I owned the national academic health workstream across forty-eight high schools, GPA, course failures, attendance, and whether a kid feels like they belong. As interim high school principal at Brooklyn Lab, instruction was part of my job. And in the third quarter, 46% of ninth graders across those schools finished at a 3.0 or better, up six points. Best quarter KIPP had ever had on that number.
11: If I'm being really honest, it's narrowing focus.

I know it takes movement on multiple fronts, operations, culture, academics, talent, teacher training. Because it's all one package deal, I can overcomplicate it and spread us too thin, and not have a few narrow, viable targets that we stack.

What I work on is building slow so we can go fast. Operating in phases. Being okay with some things being not yet. When I've done it right, like at KIPP, we shrank the change and let the early wins in our stronger regions sell the rest.

Next time I'm directly operating, the school will run off a vision that's explicit about what the first down is, what the plays are, and what every position has to do. Every player can run the touchdown, but the strategy is first downs.

I have twenty years of traditional inside school work, and I've spent the last couple of years on national strategy. 13: I figure out the one thing we're going after, and then I build the systems and tools to go after it.

I've seen this at every level. Directly at Excel on the school leadership team, as a consultant, at the network level at Collegiate and Brooklyn Lab, and nationally at KIPP. And I've made lots of mistakes at every one of them.

The first part is the most important part. What's the one thing that tells us we're on track. Then, for a school, it's clarity, investment, training, and only then accountability. The order matters. It's the Switch framework from Dan Heath, the elephant and the path.
It's a narrow focus, intense but not blind. We work on a few things, not a hundred different things. And we don't confuse action and effort with real progress.

I know how to write a system on paper. I also know that paper is worthless until the people are behind it. And the work is changing. The organizations that figure out their stance on this new tech are going to serve students better, and the ones that bury their head in the sand are going to get left behind.
It sounds like you all are very much a best idea wins culture, and that's how I work too. Strong opinions, loosely held.
